# Spring security

- Use request DTOs with Bean Validation and explicit mapping. Do not bind `@ModelAttribute`/`@RequestBody` directly to entities containing privilege or ownership fields.
- Define a default-deny `SecurityFilterChain`, order specific matchers before general ones, and use method/resource authorization for object-level decisions. Test every chain/profile.
- Disable CSRF only for genuinely stateless non-browser token APIs. Preserve CSRF protection for cookie/session authentication and browser-accessible unsafe methods.
- Configure CORS with exact allowed origins and only required methods/headers; never combine credentials with wildcard or reflected origins.
- Use Spring Data derived/bound queries or named parameters. Never concatenate JPQL/native SQL, SpEL, LDAP, or dynamic sort/property values.
- Do not parse user-controlled SpEL or expose powerful evaluation contexts. Keep Thymeleaf template/view names static and use escaped `th:text`, not untrusted `th:utext`.
- Expose only required Actuator endpoints on a protected management interface. Do not expose environment, config props, heap dump, loggers, mappings, or shutdown to untrusted networks.
- Validate JWT issuer/audience/algorithm through the supported resource-server integration. Do not merely decode claims or fetch keys from token-controlled URLs.
- Keep secrets external to `application*.properties/yml`, and prevent profile fallbacks from enabling debug, default credentials, or permissive security in production.
- Set request/upload/query/time limits and safe error responses. Keep stack traces, binding errors, framework versions, and internal management details out of client output.
